responseSet.title: A Psychoanalytic Perspective on Batterers
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

A Psychoanalytic Perspective on Batterers

Joseph Scalia M.Ed.

Joseph Scalia

300 N. Willson Avenue, Suite 3000
Bozeman, MT 59715

Joseph Scalia   Licensed counselor and a training candidate at the Colorado Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies. He was the recipient of the 1995 Gradiva Award for an earlier version of the paper published here. He is in private practice in Bozeman, MT.

This paper suggests a hypothetically necessary psychoanalytic alternative to the popular, contemporary treatments of batterers. It is argued that, in order to treat batterers, who must be understood idiographically as opposed to the stereotyping and popular monothetic viewpoints, one must attend to a number of depth-psychological factors. The preoedipal and preverbal nature of the patient must be grasped and grappled with internally by the analyst. The patient's uses of identification with the aggressor and projective identification must be understood. Especially addressed are depictions in battering of both the concealed narcissistic defense and its externalization, and a self-psychological view of the disrupted narcissistic equilibrium. Descriptions are given of pathogenic and personality aspects of battering patients, as are samples of their similarities and differences. Several treatment scenarios are provided. Acting-out pitfalls induced in the analyst are addressed, as are the need for modern psychoanalytic interventions.

Thomas Lynaugh

Thomas Lynaugh

Thomas Lynaugh  

Interpersonal psychoanalysis began not only as a reaction to the biologism of classical psychoanalytic theory but also as a protest against the theoretical dogmatism of the American Psychoanalytic Association. When the New York Institute dismissed Karen Horney as a training analyst and limited her teaching to a seminar for advanced students, Clara Thompson, in a jubilant affirmation of academic freedom, led Horney and three other faculty members out the front door singing, “Go Down, Moses.” Harry Stack Sullivan, Erich Fromm, and Frieda Fromm-Reichmann joined Thompson in creating a separate, alternative intellectual tradition within psychoanalysis.

Although there were vast conceptual differences among the founders of interpersonal psychoanalysis, they were united in their shared commitment to intellectual freedom. Over the past seventy years, they, and their followers, generated a diverse corpus of theoretical and clinical literature. There is no single unified theory of interpersonal psychoanalysis; rather, there exists a variety of theories that each claim the interpersonal field as its primordial generative structure.

William Hurst

William Hurst

William Hurst  

The French title of this study, Jacques Lacan: Esquisse d'une vie, histoire d'un système de pensée (Jacques Lacan: Outline of a Life, History of a System of Thought) by Elizabeth Roudinesco, is evidently more precise than the English, and more revealing of the nature and structure of the work. A superficial look might raise the expectation that it is essentially a biography, whereas it simply contains a sketch or an outline of a life, a sketch or an outline requiring contexts, in order to be understood. At the same time, noting that it is also a history of a system of thought, a potential reader might infer that one should expect some tough going through some highly conceptual material. In fact, though there are some elements in the material presented that would exceed the facile comprehension of most readers, Roudinesco has succeeded well in providing ready access to the contexts necessary for understanding those elements. A reader of this book will find, therefore, not only the story of Jacques Lacan, but also the story of those ideas and cultural movements within which his own story emerged. So far as I can determine, practically no major writer, artist, playwright, or philosopher who had an effect on French culture in the twentieth century is missing from these pages. They are presented, moreover, not just as influences on Lacan, but also as they developed in their own varied contexts of creativity, independently of the developing lines that came eventually to intersect the lines of Lacan's own development.

Psychoanalysis, Language, and the Body of the Text. Martin Gliserman. Gainesville, FL: University Press of Florida, 1996. 196 pp.

Elaine Hurst

Elaine Hurst

Elaine Hurst  

As Dr. Gliserman explains in the preface, “This book is about how the human body makes its appearance in those literary texts we call novels

119

and what message that body transmits” (p. ix). Contending that the body is not merely described in novels, or evoked in imagery, but is embedded in the very syntax of the text, just as DNA is preserved in amber (p. 1), Gliserman draws upon the linguistics of Chomsky, and the related fields of syntactics and semantics, to develop his study of the multiplicity of levels in which the body is manifested in those representative novels he considers. As he “deconstructs” the texts, he forges a connection between these linguistic approaches and the psychoanalytic understanding of the conscious and unconscious manifestations of the body in language. Essentially, what Dr. Gliserman seems to be attempting to do, is to shed light on the “mind-body problem” through an unpacking of the intricately interwoven verbal, symbolic, and nonverbal communications which come forth in a good novel. Almost coincidentally, Dr. Gliserman points out, his analysis of the works selected leads him to a study of trauma, which frequently serves as a theme in literature, and which cuts to the heart of the mind-body connection, through the breaking down of the boundaries of defense which we erect.

It is Gliserman's thesis that an author's style is not merely an artifice, but rather (beyond its consciously crafted language) an unconscious expression of a deeper, bodily (nonverbal) message. He declares: “A novel articulates a body as much as it tells a story. It develops a preverbal, ur-gender, nonverbal and/or unverbalized visceral experience as much as it develops an intricate symbolic interpersonal interaction in a complex setting over space and time” (p. 3). He cites the contributions which feminist writers have made to the awareness of the bodily messages, and the gender-specific communications which are to be found in literature, but he also notes the more universal (and perhaps more primitive) configurations which emerge in the texts of both male and female authors. In the four novels he studies (Daniel Defoe's Robinson Crusoe, Charlotte Bronte's Jane Eyre, Virginia Woolf's To the Lighthouse, and David Bradley's The Chaneysville Incident), Gliserman points out that “All the texts show the tension between trauma and creativity… [and] although the male and female characters in these texts play out their separate gendered roles, within the deeper forms of the fiction the bodies are reconfigured in nonconventional ways” (p. 9). Often, he explains, the central drama of the novel focuses on the tension between integration and fragmentation, reflecting the Freudian dialectic between Eros and Thanatos as well as the Kleinian conflict “between rage and destruction, and guilt and reparation” (p. 56).

Robert Marshall

Robert Marshall  

This is a valuable book not only for child and adolescent therapists, but for clinicians interested in countertransference. The papers stem from a congress of The European Federation for Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy in Public Health Services. The particular merits of the book are the insights into the use of countertransference from clinicians trained and practicing under different circumstances in six countries: England, Greece, France, Germany, Belgium, and Switzerland. Moreover, we are treated to clinical accounts from the Tavistock Clinic and the Anna Freud Centre. Treatment of neurotics, borderlines, and psychotics is explicated as well. While most of the accounts are about outpatient treatment, there is an important chapter on inpatient problems. In addition, we are privy to an excellent exposition of a rare topic—countertransference toward parents. The authors courageously provide rather copious clinical reports of their work as well as their dynamic analyses. The reader has opportunity to appraise the work as well as develop one's own hypotheses about the cases.

The editors have spared us the familiar review of the history of countertransference in each of these articles, but provide one solid chapter about the clinicians who are influencing European thought. American authors are well represented.

The following is based on the inaugural commencement address held at the Boston Graduate School for Psychoanalysis, the first free-standing psychoanalytic training institute chartered to grant a master's degree in psychoanalysis. The paper briefly reviews the development of psychoanalysis and the issue of autonomy. It also recapitulates the evolution of psychoanalytic training institutes within the United States. It then examines and speculates on possible directions psychoanalysis will take in the upcoming century.

Projection and Projective Indentification in a Three-Year-Old Boy

Dan Gilhooley MA

Dan Gilhooley

46 North Howells Point Road
Bellport, NY 11713

Dan Gilhooley   Private practice in New York City. He is also an artist, an educator, a graduate of the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis, and a certificate candidate at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies. In 1995, he won NAAP's Gradiva Award for visual art.

Observations of a three-year-old boy are interpreted in terms of the psychoanalytic concept of projection as articulated by Sigmund Freud, as well as Melanie Klein's theory of projective identification. The author concludes that the projective mechanisms described by freud and Klein are both useful tools for understanding this young boy's behavior, and proposes that these projective processes are qualitatively different, having emerged in this young subject at different periods of emotional development, and are unconsciously employed by the boy to accomplish different objectives. Projection was employed by this young child as an ego defense warding off intolerable feelings and self-representations. Requiring a complex use of verbal explanation, projection is a developmentally more advanced process than projective identification which involves the nonverbal emotional communication of an unconscious fantasy. Where projection is an intrapsychic process employed at moments of relative ego autonomy, projective identification is used by this young boy to strengthen his narcissistic attachment to objects, and to fuse together libidinal and aggressive drives to simultaneously hate and preserve these objects.

The fifty-first volume of The Psychoanalytic Study of the Child commemorates the one-hundredth birthday of Anna Freud, one of its founders. The first five articles in this compendium, by Clifford Yorke, Samuel Abrams, Peter Neubauer, Joseph and Sonja Goldstein, and Elisabeth Young-Bruehl, are papers presented at a symposium at Yale University in honor of Ms. Freud's centenary in December 1995. Other papers comment on Anna Freud with regard to psychoanalytic theory as well as the theory of child development. These are followed by a series of clinical contributions and a section on applied child psychoanalysis.

Yorke reminds us of how aware Ms. Freud was of the fast-changing nature of the child's “average expectable environment” in the latter part of the twentieth century (p. 21). Not only did she flesh out the mechanisms of defense discovered by her father, but went on to make a contribution of inestimable richness based on her intensive and extensive work with young and ever younger children, culminating in a theory of developmental lines and the construction of the Developmental Profile.

Writing about Anna Freud's theory and technique, Jill Miller tells us that in assessing the level of development a child has attained one has to ask the (seemingly simple) question, “is he where he needs to be and what is holding him up?” (p. 149) Miller tells us of Ms. Freud's ongoing concerns about whether early deficits are treatable and reversible and, if so, by what means.

Neubauer emphasizes how Anna Freud's experience led her to conclude that child analysis was concerned with treatment beyond neurosis by quoting from her 1974 paper to this effect:

If we accept the view that childhood psychopathology has a twofold causation, one rooted in the conflicts, defense, and compromise formations, the other in the developmental processes, we have no reason to believe that the same therapeutic measures will be equally effective for both.

Clinical Observations on Premature Termination in Group Analysis

Leslie Rosenthal PHD

Leslie Rosenthal

12 West 96th Street
New York, NY 10025

Leslie Rosenthal   Dean of Group Psychoanalytic Studies at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies. He has served as Group Therapy Consultant to a wide variety of social agencies, hospitals, and educational institutions. His book, The Resolution of Resistance in Group Psychotherapy, was published by Jason Aronson.

The problem of premature termination is addressed as a pervasively critical issue in group treatment. The phenomenon of dropouts and castouts is as old as man, from the casting out of Adam and Eve, Esau and Joseph, to the dropping out of Benedict Arnold and Timothy McVeigh. The literature on premature termination is reviewed, and its emphasis on inadequate preparation of members, feelings of alienation from the group, and the role of early provocateurs is noted. The role of the therapist in contributing to loss of members is examined in terms of insufficient understanding of members' nuclear dynamics and countertransference resistances. The vulnerability of new members to group hostility and to subsequent expulsion is recognized. The exposure of members and groups to toxic dosages of emotional stimulation is identified as a frequent dynamic in premature termination. The crucial task of the therapist in monitoring the level of such exposure is stressed. The significant role of the screening process in identifying potential dropouts is illustrated, and measures to prevent defections from the group are offered.

Communication between patient and analyst is a two-way transaction. The communication may be verbal or nonverbal, conscious or unconscious. Our earliest mode of communication is through behaviors and sounds. In adult life this mode persists, so that our spoken communications may often be accompanied by unspoken messages. In the analytic situation, unspoken messages are an integral part of the communications from patient to analyst and analyst to patient. Examples are presented of spoken and unspoken communications, and their role in the psychoanalytic process is explained.

Siamak Movahedi PHD

Siamak Movahedi

Siamak Movahedi   Faculty of the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis and the University of Massachusetts, Boston.

No other discipline as much as psychoanalysis is caught in the elusive web of time and history. It is even claimed that time is the most fundamental dimension of psychic reality. Yet, psychoanalysis remains an a historical and dynamic method of analysis of mind in the “here-and-now.” In this paper I shall try to explore the relationship between time and psychic reality. Then, I shall examine the temporal structure of the analytic situation, and try to decipher the transferential meaning of the recall of past events in analysis.

Dreams from several patients are discussed to demonstrate the communication of aggression turned against the self. The analysis of the communications is based on the symbols and actions in the dreams, the talk in the sessions, and the induced feelings. Some discussion of transference and countertransference is also included. The aggression is discussed in terms of its magnitude, form, and pattern of discharge. Some conclusions are drawn regarding the nature of a therapeutic response in each case.

This slim volume contains a rich collection of papers delivered at the 25th Annual Margaret Mahler Symposium in 1994 on developmental and clinical aspects of aggression by psychoanalysts Harold Blum, Otto Kernberg, Selma Kramer, and Fred Pine. The discussions of these papers by Salman Akhtar, Dorothy Holmes, Peter Neubauer, and Henri Parens are interesting contributions in their own right.

In the first contribution Kramer observes that the descriptions of the Oedipus complex have customarily emphasized the child's aggressive and libidinal impulses toward the parents, but that the other side of this issue—parental hatred toward children—has largely been ignored. Noting that in the classical Oedipus myth it was Laius who planned the murder of his three-day-old son, she presents the phenomenon of filicide: parental aggression that was held in check as long as the child was helpless and dependent, can be activated and break through at the advent of puberty. Kramer notes that it is largely older male political leaders and legislators who send mostly male children off to war. Case vignettes are offered illustrating that fathers who suffered abuse from their own fathers are driven through identification with the aggressor to relate similarly to their sons.

Blum carefully traces the lengthy process by which the establishment of impulse control and superego development occurs in children. He then offers the concept of “sanctified aggression” where instead of being regarded as a threat to the self or object, hatred may be authorized, rationalized, and justified. He suggests, “Because hate is so destructive to familial and group cohesion, it is easily displaced and projected outside the family or the group” (p. 23). Blum continues that there is no simple relationship between hate and rage though they are usually bound together. A rage center is found in the human brain near the hypothalamic locus for sexual excitement. No such locus is known for the attitude of hate. Hate may be present without rage but rage is probably associated with or alloyed by some aspect of hate. Blum suggests that the superego is never fully autonomous: it is easily suspended or submerged by introjection of new external authority. Standards and values that were once cherished can be shunted aside with ego justification, rationalization, and societal sanction, processes which legitimized the Holocaust.

Neville Symington brings intense personal conviction to this volume on the training and maturation of a psychological healer and the professional dilemmas facing the field of psychotherapy today. A distillation from eight years of lectures for psychiatrists and psychoanalysts, mostly in Australia and New Zealand, the book represents Symington's efforts to integrate disparate theories of the mind and technique garnered in study, teaching, and practice in Britain and in Australia.

This is no small task. Central to the dialectic of his discussions are the tensions of opposing theories and points of view rigidly held. For example he points to the tabula rasa theory of personality, created by environment acting upon the innocent, whose reactions form core character patterns—a theory in which he was well and deeply indoctrinated in his English training. He then alludes to the opposite proposition— responsiveness to and creation of environment by psychic actions—which he has deeply digested in Australia, where he now lives and works. In the face of such examples, Symington, from wide mastery of the writings of psychoanalysis, religion, literature, and philosophy, and much clinical experience, invariably concludes that both static theoretical positions are incorrect. He critiques the logical conclusions and behavioral and emotional sequelae

This article seeks to compare the theories and techniques of Hyman Spotnitz and Heinz Kohut. Both clinicians have founded schools of psychoanalysis, namely, modern psychoanalysis and self psychology. Both clinicians have been recognized as having successfully treated the bane of Freud's therapeutic endeavors, the narcissistic neuroses. At the same time, there has been little communication between the aforementioned schools.

Bernstein (1986) compared Spotnitz and Kohut along the three obstacles Freud thought rendered the narcissistic patient untreatable: indifference, hostility, and the absence of a coherent ego. She concluded that there was considerable overlap between the two systems. The present article builds on Bernstein's work and Detrick and Detrick's (1989) volume in which Kohut is compared to twenty other clinicians.

Joan Hertz PHD

Joan Hertz

400 S. Oyster Bay Road
Hicksville, NY 11801

Joan Hertz   Psychoanalyst in private practice in Hicksville, NY. She is a graduate of Adelphi University School of Social Work, The Union Institute, and The Long Island Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies, and is author of In Pursuit of Authenticity—An Adoptee's Quest: A Comparative Study of the Transference Before and After Reunion.

Because adoptees tend to believe that their innate defectiveness, not the chosen-child story, was the real reason they were relinquished by their birth parents, they often develop defenses which protect them from another abandonment, this time by their adoptive families. To assimilate, adoptees typically develop the as-if personality, compromising themselves in order to fit in with a biologically alien family. Sealed records leave adoptees in a state of genealogical bewilderment with no knowledge of their ancestry, inherent talents, or biological weaknesses. The urgency to resolve this through a successful search is offset by the loss of the fantasy mother and the risk of being rejected by her again. The following study explores the seven-year analysis of an adopted woman who was reunited with her birth parents during the course of treatment to assess whether establishing her biological roots and, thereby, having a more authentic sense of self, can ameliorate the as-if defense.

In conducting this study, particular attention was paid to the split transference. The analysand's ability to express anger spontaneously in session was a measure of authenticity before and after the search. The question of whether full integration of the personality is dependent upon establishing biological roots is the thrust of this research.

One-Person or Two-Person Psychology?

Jacob Kirman PHD

Jacob Kirman

254 East 68th Street
New York, NY 10021

Jacob Kirman   Psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City and a Professor of psychology at Queens College of CUNY. He is training and control analyst, and a faculty member at the Center for Modern Psychoanalytic Studies.

Analysts who espouse a two-person psychology characterize classical psychoanalysis as a one-person psychology, which fails to recognize the inevitability of interaction and mutual influence in the analytic relationship. They claim that this one-person view maintains an outmoded conception that the analyst is in a privileged position to observe and interpret the patient's unconscious impulses, defenses, and resistances. They refute the classical view that the analyst can function as a blank screen, upon which the patient's transference is projected. Two-person analysts emphasize the limitations of the analyst's knowledge, the analyst's unavoidable self-revelation, and inescapable involvement in the patient's transference and resistance. Some recommend that analysts utilize self-disclosure as a principle of technique, minimize the analyst's unwarranted authority, and encourage mutual examination of all issues by patient and analyst. These recommendations are discussed and critically examined from the point of view of modern analysis.

Eugene Goldwater   Psychiatrist and psychoanalyst who practices in Holyoke and Brookline, MA. He is a faculty member at the Boston Graduate School of Psychoanalysis.

Freud wrote extensively about men's feelings of hate and fear toward other men, but had little understanding of men's hate and fear toward women. The present author, having previously (Goldwater, 1990) begun to look at men's hate toward women, now turns to men's fear of women. In order to make this even more painful and difficult subject bearable, to himself and to others, he utilizes humor and other avoidant techniques, so readers may choose for themselves just how seriously they wish to contemplate the issue.

In summary, men suffer from two powerful, but largely unconscious fears with respect to women. The first, an ancient one, stems from the ability of women to bring new life into the world, and the perception that they are able to control men's sexuality for that and other purposes. The second, a product of modern society, is that in the world of the future, men will no longer be necessary—a thought which gives men a strong impetus to violence.

The story of Oedipus is retold, replacing Freud's feminophilic attitude with a feminophobic one in order to demonstrate the need for psychoanalysts to consider both perspectives in their work. Finally, the author acknowledges his failure to come up with nontrivial solutions either to men's short-term dilemmas over trusting women, or to the long-term issue of the place of men in a woman's world.

The need to feel loved, as distinct from to be loved, is universal, and the conditions for its satisfaction are highly specific for each individual. This need, when unmet, mobilizes the need to hate. When these two tendencies are not resolved in the course of development they are treated as resistances to maturation. Their resolution in the analysis is achieved through the use of modern psychoanalytic techniques based on emotional understanding and emotional communication, and are aimed at facilitating the appropriate release of frustration-aggression and on supplying the nurturing function within the analytic framework. The passive aim to feel loved gives way to the active aim “I want to love.” Case material is presented throughout to illustrate relevant dynamics and the approach to treatment.

In a study on obsessive love and attachment disorders, subjects described experiences of acute rejection, powerlessness, and inner emptiness. The experiences of obsessions with an unavailable or rejecting partner persisted for months or years, and were often accompanied by violent impulses and/or suicidal fantasies. Subjects demonstrated depressive/addictive traits, strong narcissistic features, and schizoid defenses. This author suggests that tenacious love-obsessions signify an internalized, preoedipal attachment disturbance—a morbid attachment to the “missing” object of infancy. These patients typically have difficulty forming an attachment bond with the analyst, perceiving the analyst as a dangerous, rejecting agent who will recapitulate the original trauma. Using the clinical example of “Gretchen's Obsession,” the author employs modern analytic techniques of “joining” and “mirroring” (Spotnitz, 1976), as well as Winnicott's (1960b) concept of “holding” to create a progressive therapeutic bond, as toxic resistant forces are gradually resolved.

[[RunningHead]]

The Seed of Madness: Constitution, Environment, and Fantasy in The Organization of the Psychotic Core. V.D. Volkan & S. Akhtar, eds. Madison, CT: International Universities Press, 1997. 213 pp.

Jane Snyder

Jane Snyder

Jane Snyder  

In this collection of papers, psychoanalysts grapple with the nature of psychosis using an object relational framework to understand preobject states, the development of mind, and the “seed” of psychosis. Introductory and concluding chapters by Volkan and Akhtar respectively provide a theoretical envelope for the mostly case-based chapters within the volume, with two contributors developing further aspects of theory. Volkan proposes that the “mad seed,” a psychotic core, develops from the early mother-object undifferentiated matrix in which mind “incubates.” The “core self” develops from this flux of early experience and images as early ego mechanisms (projection, introjection) are used to establish a separation of self and object. When this fails to occur, there is a lack of differentiation and a continued reliance on primitive mechanisms, resulting in a psychotic core. Volkan ascribes this failure to the nature of the “affect saturating the core self”—if “bad” (rage, terror, envy, aggression) and there is an absence of “good” affects to modulate, a “mad seed” develops. In the summary chapter Akhtar acknowledges the role of genetics, but notes the importance of the early mothering environment to help the infant insulate the primitive ego from overstimulation, to regulate affect and establish internal homeostasis. Otherwise the infant is in constant distress, even panic; affect is unmanageable, and excessive aggression is directed toward the self, particularly on “linking” (in the sense described by Bion), the forming of mental connections. This “mad seed” may result in full blown psychosis, or remain encapsulated, or disappear “if a libidinally dominated seed develops” to offset it. If the mad seed dominates the personality, reality will be constructed and used to enact parts of the psychotic self. The analytic solution according to Volkan is to provide a “libidinal seed” through the analyst-analysand relationship, but first to reexperience and master the “bad affects.
